name: University Club Sponsorship Proposal
description: A high-energy campus sponsorship proposal for presenting a student organization, flagship event, audience evidence, measurable exposure inventory, tiered packages, and an owner-led execution plan.
style_guide:
# University Club Sponsorship Proposal

## Visual concept

Create a bold, sponsor-ready proposal for a university club, student organization, campus festival, conference, competition, performance, or community event. The visual language is a dark live-event control room: near-black violet canvas, saturated pink and purple identity, cyan execution signals, selective yellow and green asset categories, oversized white conclusions, event photography, modular inventory cards, tier comparisons, and a dated activation timeline.

The previews are visual references only. Do not copy their club, event, audience, attendance, social reach, budget, vendors, programming, impressions, rates, package names, dates, partner rights, or contacts. Build every commercial and operational claim from current evidence.

## Canvas, grid, and safe area

- Use a fixed `1280 × 720 px` 16:9 canvas with `48–58 px` side margins, `24–32 px` top framing, and `22–28 px` for sources and page numbering.
- Use a 12-column grid with `14–18 px` gutters. Align club and event cards, audience charts, program lists, exposure inventory, package columns, timeline nodes, and next-step actions.
- Reserve `88–118 px` for section label, sponsor-facing headline, and one concise commercial implication.
- Prefer photographic full-bleed covers, balanced `6/6` club-and-event pages, donut-plus-program layouts, `3 × 2` asset grids, three-tier package columns, and full-width activation timelines.
- Use `14–20 px` between large modules and `8–12 px` within cards. Keep event energy without sacrificing rate and rights legibility.

## Color system

### Core colors

- Event midnight: `#0C081C`. Use for the main canvas and deepest card surfaces.
- Headline white: `#F8F6F5`. Use for conclusions, tier names, key values, and essential labels.
- Campus pink: `#F735A4`. Use for brand identity, primary reach, title sponsorship, and major attention points.
- Electric purple: `#7255FF`. Use for presenting-partner assets, audience series, and secondary identity.
- Live cyan: `#1FC9EC`. Use for execution timing, digital inventory, active steps, and reporting.
- Asset yellow: `#FFB43C`. Use for sampling, physical activation, or supporting tiers.
- Completion green: `#49D68C`. Use only for confirmed readiness or completed operational steps.

### Usage rules

- Pink and purple carry the event identity. Cyan carries execution and measurable digital delivery.
- Yellow and green should categorize specific assets, not decorate every page.
- Keep white dominant for reading and maintain high contrast on all dark cards.
- Use red only for a real blocker, capacity issue, or unapproved item.

## Typography

- Use `Inter`, `Arial`, `Aptos Display`, or another bold geometric sans-serif.
- Cover title: `54–70 px`, bold; page headline: `34–44 px`, bold; key values: `30–44 px`; body: `13–16 px`; package details: `10–13 px`; sources: `8–10 px`.
- Use `IBM Plex Mono` or a similar mono face for section codes, dates, inventory identifiers, availability, and source notes.
- Use tabular numerals for attendance, reach, impressions, rates, dates, duration, and capacity.
- Keep sponsor language direct and avoid long paragraphs or youth-marketing clichés.

## Layout and component language

- Cards use dark violet or black fills, thin colored top rules, square corners, and no shadow.
- Club and event overview cards should distinguish organization scale, event scope, audience, program, timing, and operational capacity.
- Exposure cards require asset, location or channel, quantity, timing, projected delivery, production owner, and measurement method.
- Package columns must share one row structure so rights and differences are directly comparable.
- Use color-coded check marks only after the corresponding entitlement is written in text.
- Next-step panels should show action, owner, due date, required input, and decision gate.

## Charts and data

- Favor audience donuts, demographic bars, programming lists, reach or impression cards, asset inventories, tier comparisons, and activation timelines.
- Define attendance, reach, impressions, views, followers, subscribers, footfall, product trials, and engagement separately.
- Show actual historical delivery separately from forecast or capacity. State source year, sample, platform, and estimation method.
- Avoid stacked reach totals that double-count the same students across channels.
- Do not use 3D charts, decorative funnels, or audience claims that cannot be verified.

## Page variations

### Partnership invitation cover

Use an event photograph with a dark magenta-violet overlay. Lead with the shared campus-and-brand opportunity, then show presenter, organization, date, version, confidentiality, and one verified reach statement.

### Club and flagship event overview

Pair organization context with a clearly bounded flagship event. Show membership, chapters, program cadence, event date, format, attendance capacity, vendors, and duration only when supported.

### Audience and event highlights

Use a demographic or audience chart beside programming pillars. Make the sponsor-relevant insight explicit without stereotyping students or overstating purchasing power.

### Sponsor value and exposure assets

Use a six-card asset grid covering physical, stage, content, newsletter, recap, creator, sampling, or other real channels. Each card must state delivery and measurement.

### Sponsorship packages and benefits

Use three directly comparable tiers with capped availability, prices, rights, production requirements, exclusivity, and optional add-ons. Highlight a recommended tier only when the fit is justified.

### Execution timeline and next steps

Show contract, creative lock, production, rehearsal, event, recap, reporting, and renewal stages. Finish with three immediate actions and the responsible contact.

## Imagery and icons

- Use rights-cleared photographs of the real event, campus venue, audience, stage, activation, speakers, performers, volunteers, and sponsor placements.
- Preserve natural diversity and obtain required participant and campus permissions.
- Use one geometric icon family for stage, audio, sampling, creator content, newsletter, photo, video, contract, and report.
- Avoid unrelated concert crowds, fake sponsor mockups, unlicensed campus marks, stock students presented as attendees, and images of unsafe or prohibited activity.

## Content integrity

- Do not invent membership, attendance, demographics, followers, budget, program counts, impressions, reach, vendors, sponsor results, rates, inventory, availability, or timelines.
- Separate audited, organizer-recorded, platform-reported, surveyed, estimated, projected, and guaranteed delivery.
- State whether reach is unique, cumulative, organic, paid, whitelisted, or cross-platform and explain overlap limits.
- Secure permission for university names, logos, venues, participant imagery, mailing lists, alcohol or age-restricted activity, and sponsor categories.
- Define category exclusivity, cancellation, force majeure, creative approval, production cost, tax, payment, make-good, reporting, and renewal terms.
- If evidence is unavailable, omit it or label it `estimate`, `forecast`, `proposed`, `capacity`, `subject to approval`, or `to be confirmed`.

## Avoid

- Do not copy preview organization, event, audience, rates, packages, inventory, metrics, dates, vendors, or contacts.
- Do not sell the same exclusive right to multiple partners or promise inventory the university has not approved.
- Do not combine followers, attendees, views, and impressions into one undifferentiated reach number.
- Do not stereotype students or imply campus endorsement, data access, or purchase behavior without evidence and permission.
- Do not use every accent color on every card; category color must remain meaningful.
- Do not use glossy glass effects, heavy glow, oversized rounded corners, 3D charts, tiny package terms, or decorative neon that harms readability.
